stories.headline: SoftBank's Son explored, then dropped, $1T SK Hynix bid
stories.move: SoftBank CEO Masayoshi Son recently approached Wall Street banks about financing a roughly $1 trillion buyout of South Korean memory-chip maker SK Hynix, The Information reported Nov. 20. SK Hynix closed around 777.5 trillion won (about $577 billion) that Friday, so the figure implied roughly a 73% premium. A SoftBank spokesperson said the idea 'is no longer under active consideration.' SK Hynix said it 'knows nothing at all about the matter.'
stories.why: SK Hynix is one of three main suppliers of the high-bandwidth memory chips AI accelerators need, alongside Samsung and Micron, fitting Son's push to control more of the AI hardware stack after SoftBank's Ampere and OpenAI bets.
stories.bear: SoftBank had about 5.39 trillion yen (roughly $34.3 billion) in cash at the end of September, about 3% of the bid size, and Korean law requires government approval for any foreign takeover of SK Hynix, which a senior official said would be a tough sell politically.
stories.watch: Whether SoftBank revisits SK Hynix or another large AI-hardware target once financing or politics look friendlier.

stories.headline: Chip stocks give back Monday's Jensen Huang rally
stories.move: Nvidia closed down 5.86% and AMD closed down 8.86% on Nov. 24, giving back part of Monday's rally that followed Nvidia's board reinstating Jensen Huang as CEO. Intel fell 8.15%, Broadcom fell 3.98% and Micron fell 11.01% the same day. The Nasdaq-100 fund QQQ closed down 1.99% and the S&P 500 fund SPY fell 0.49%, while the Dow fund DIA rose 0.79%.
stories.why: Chip stocks gave back part of Monday's sharp gains; UBS's Mark Haefele said the swings were not a signal that the 'structural AI investment story has broken.'
stories.bear: A one-day pullback after Monday's rally is itself unremarkable, but Nvidia stock is still well below where it traded before Huang's Nov. 12 resignation, showing the leadership episode left a lasting dent.
stories.watch: Wednesday's GDP and inflation reports, and whether chip stocks stabilize or keep giving back Monday's gains.

stories.headline: Peter Thiel buys $122 million more of Palantir stock
stories.move: Peter Thiel bought 850,100 Palantir Class A shares for about $122.3 million in three open-market purchases on Nov. 20, paying between $142.91 and $144.61 a share, according to a Form 4 filed Nov. 24. He held none of the shares directly before the purchases.
stories.why: The buy is Thiel's first disclosed personal purchase of Palantir stock in recent filings; it comes after he sold nearly 2 million shares under a 10b5-1 trading plan in March.
stories.bear: The $122 million is a small fraction of Thiel's overall Palantir exposure, most of which sits in entities like Rivendell 7 LLC and PLTR Holdings LLC, so the buy may say less about his conviction than the dollar figure suggests.
stories.watch: Further Form 4 filings showing whether Thiel keeps buying or returns to selling under a new 10b5-1 plan.

stories.headline: Blackstone-backed Medline sells $2.1B more stock
stories.move: Medline priced a secondary offering of 60 million Class A shares at $35.50 each on Nov. 17, worth about $2.1 billion, sold entirely by stockholders tied to Blackstone, Carlyle, Hellman & Friedman, GIC and an Abu Dhabi Investment Authority subsidiary; Medline itself gets none of the proceeds. The sale was set to close Nov. 23. A Form 4 for Stephen Schwarzman, filed Nov. 19, shows Blackstone-linked entities converting about 7.57 million Medline Class B shares into Class A shares on Nov. 17-18 to enable the sale.
stories.why: It's the second time this year Medline's private-equity sponsors have sold down their stake, following the company's record $6.26 billion IPO in December 2025, as the backers use strong markets to cash out of their 2021 buyout.
stories.bear: Repeated large secondary sales by the same sponsors can weigh on a stock even when the underlying business is healthy, since they signal insiders are steadily reducing their exposure.
stories.watch: Whether Blackstone, Carlyle and Hellman & Friedman sell down further once any post-offering lockup lifts.

stories.headline: Tether leaders add $5.7 million more to Gold.com stake
stories.move: Tether International, S.A. de C.V. - controlled by Tether Global Investments Fund and, ultimately, Giancarlo Devasini, Jean-Louis van der Velde and Paolo Ardoino - bought 150,000 more Gold.com shares for about $5.75 million at $38.31 each on Nov. 23, per Forms 4 filed Nov. 25. That brings its direct Gold.com stake to 650,000 shares, separate from 3,370,787 shares the group holds through another Tether entity, TPM, S.A. de C.V.
stories.why: Tether has been steadily adding to Gold.com, a precious-metals dealer, since a roughly $150 million PIPE deal in February, part of its broader push into gold-backed and real-world assets alongside its USDT stablecoin business.
stories.bear: At $5.75 million, the purchase is tiny next to Tether's existing Gold.com position, so it may be routine portfolio management rather than a fresh strategic signal.
stories.watch: Further Form 4 filings from Tether entities in Gold.com and its other public holdings.

stories.via: Blackstone Private Real Estate Credit & Income Fund
stories.headline: Schwarzman buys $10 million more of a Blackstone fund
stories.move: Stephen Schwarzman bought 388,224 shares of Blackstone Private Real Estate Credit & Income Fund for about $10.2 million at $26.16 each on Nov. 20, split between two purchases, according to a Form 4 filed Nov. 23.
stories.why: The purchase adds to Schwarzman's personal stake in one of Blackstone's retail-facing private credit vehicles, which invests in real estate debt rather than equity.
stories.bear: As Blackstone's chairman and CEO, Schwarzman has an obvious incentive to support demand for the firm's own funds, so a personal purchase is not necessarily a read on the broader real estate credit market.
stories.watch: Flows into Blackstone's non-traded real estate credit funds, a business the firm has been expanding to individual investors.

stories.headline: Berkshire raises ¥182 billion in new yen bonds
stories.move: Berkshire Hathaway issued five series of yen-denominated senior notes totaling ¥182.3 billion (roughly $1.2 billion) on Nov. 19, ranging from notes due 2029 at 2.624% to notes due 2056 at 4.571%, according to an 8-K filing. Mizuho Securities USA and Merrill Lynch International underwrote the deal under Berkshire's existing shelf registration.
stories.why: Berkshire regularly taps the yen bond market, where its borrowing costs are low, to fund acquisitions and operations without touching its large cash pile.
stories.bear: More debt, even cheap debt, adds to Berkshire's balance sheet at a time its insurance earnings have already been falling, including at GEICO.
stories.watch: How Berkshire deploys the proceeds, and whether it returns to the yen market again given its history of regular issuance there.
